chapter.title: Rexx Classes for .NET
chapter.para: A Rexx class can be a .NET class: .net~extend makes a .NET type whose overrides are the class's methods. .NET code then uses Rexx objects where it wants its own types: a comparer for its sorts, an observable object for a user interface, a writer for its output.

section.title: A Comparer for .NET's Sorts
section.para: You want to give .NET an object that implements one of its interfaces.

example.title: A Comparer for .NET's Sorts
example.programlisting:
.net~extend(.ByLength, "System.Collections.Generic.IComparer<System.String>") list = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<System.String>")~new do w over "ccc a bb dddd"~makeArray(" "); list~Add(w); end list~Sort(.ByLength~new) say list~ToArray~makeString("L", " ") sorted = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.SortedSet<System.String>")~new(.ByLength~new) do w over "kiwi fig banana"~makeArray(" "); sorted~Add(w); end say sorted~makeArray~makeString("L", " ")
::requires "net.cls" ::class ByLength subclass NetObject ::method Compare use arg a, b return sign(a~length - b~length)
example.screen: a bb ccc dddd fig kiwi banana

section.para: How it works. .net~extend(.ByLength, "System.Collections.Generic.IComparer<System.String>") makes a .NET type that implements the interface with the class's methods: Compare is IComparer.Compare. .ByLength~new is then a Rexx object and a .NET object at once, which .NET's Sort and SortedSet use as any comparer. The class must be a subclass of NetObject.
See also Reference, Rexx Classes and .NET Classes.

section.title: An Observable Object
section.para: You want an object whose changes .NET code (a WPF binding) can watch.

example.title: An Observable Object
example.programlisting:
p = .Person~new p~PropertyChanged += .net~handler(.Watcher~new, "CHANGED") p~setName("Ann") p~setName("Bob")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Person subclass NetObject ::method activate class .net~extend(self, "System.ComponentModel.INotifyPropertyChanged") ::method setName expose name use arg name args = .net~System~ComponentModel~PropertyChangedEventArgs~new("Name") self~raise.PropertyChanged(self, args) ::method name expose name return name ::class Watcher ::method changed use arg sender, e say e~PropertyName "is now" sender~name
example.screen: Name is now Ann Name is now Bob

section.para: How it works. An interface's event is an event of the new type, which any .NET code, and Rexx code, can subscribe to. The object raises it with self~raise.PropertyChanged(...), a private method that only its own methods can call, as in C#. The class's activate class method extends it when the class is created, before any instance.
See also Reference, Rexx Classes and .NET Classes, Generic Methods, ref and out, Events.

section.title: Overriding a .NET Class
section.para: You want a .NET class whose behaviour is changed in Rexx, as a C# subclass changes it.

example.title: Overriding a .NET Class
example.programlisting:
c = .Shouting~new c~Add("hello"); c~Insert(0, "world") say c[0] c[1] c~Count
::requires "net.cls" ::class Shouting subclass NetObject ::method activate class .net~extend(self, "System.Collections.ObjectModel.Collection<System.String>") ::method InsertItem -- protected virtual void InsertItem(int index, string item) use arg index, item self~InsertItem:super(index, item~upper)

section.para: How it works. Collection<T> calls its protected virtual InsertItem for every Add and Insert; the Rexx method overrides it, and self~InsertItem:super(...) calls the base's implementation, C#'s base.InsertItem. On Windows, the sample windows/forms-extend.rex is a Form whose OnPaint and OnResize are Rexx methods.
See also Reference, Rexx Classes and .NET Classes.
